label: Lesson 12
title: Coupled chemistry and coulometry
summary: Real electrode reactions are rarely alone. The product of a faradaic step often reacts again in solution before it can migrate away, or the reactant is regenerated by an upstream reaction. These coupled homogeneous reactions distort every trace we have met - the voltammogram, the chronoamperometric current, the impedance spectrum - and learning to read those distortions is how mechanisms are solved. The lesson then scales the same chemistry up: bulk electrolysis, coulometry as analysis, and the engineering shape of a reactor.

intro.text: Until now we have assumed one reaction at the electrode: O + ne reversibly gives R. That is the exception, not the rule. In a real cell the product R usually lives in a reactive solution, and the analyte O is often produced or consumed by reactions that never touch the electrode. The electrode's job is then less a single step and more the first move of a sequence.

Following Bagotsky ch.17-18 and Bard & Faulkner ch.11-12 we first classify those sequences - EC, CE, ECE, catalytic - and show exactly how each one bends a voltammogram. Then we scale the same chemistry up: bulk electrolysis to completion, coulometry as an absolute analytical method, and the reactor design questions that decide what a process is allowed to cost.

intro.title: The one-sentence summary of this lesson
intro.body: Homogeneous chemistry coupled to a faradaic step leaves a fingerprint on every voltammetric trace; reading that fingerprint is mechanistic analysis, and running the sequence to exhaustion is coulometric analysis - the two sides of one coin.

sections.title: When the electrode is not alone
sections.summary: Most real reactions are sequences: an electron-transfer step followed, preceded, or accompanied by homogeneous chemistry. Those couplings hide in the shape of the current-time curve.
keyPoints: An EC reaction is an electron transfer followed by a homogeneous reaction that consumes the product.
A CE reaction is a homogeneous reaction that makes the electroactive species, which the electrode then consumes.
An ECE reaction alternates electron transfers and chemical steps.
A catalytic scheme regenerates the reactant at the electrode, so the current is carried by a fast-cycling mediator.

blocks.text: Picture the electrode as only one actor in the story. The electron-transfer step is the scene it owns; everything else happens in the solution around it. A product made at the surface may decompose, dimerise, or react with the solvent. A reactant may have to be produced by a prior hydrolysis or dissociation. The electrode only reports what it sees, but what it sees has been filtered by the chemistry around it.

The shorthand for those filters is a string of letters. E is an electron-transfer step at the electrode; C is a homogeneous chemical step in solution. Read them in order and you have the mechanism. The four you will meet most often are:

items: **EC** - an electron transfer, then a homogeneous reaction that consumes the product. The return wave shrinks.
**CE** - a homogeneous reaction makes the electroactive species first, then the electrode takes it. The forward wave can be fed by the chemical step.
**ECE** - electron transfer, chemical step, then a second electron transfer at the electrode.
**Catalytic** - the reactant is regenerated by a chemical step, so one molecule of mediator turns over many times of current.

blocks.text: The diagnostic question is always the same: if I slow down and squint at the experiment, what does the coupled step do to the trace? Does the reverse peak still come back? Does the forward peak grow differently with scan rate? Is the limiting current bigger than one electron's worth? The next two sections work those answers through.

sections.title: The EC fingerprint on a voltammogram
sections.summary: A following chemical reaction eats the product of the electron-transfer step. Its effect depends on the competition between the chemical clock and the experimental timescale.
keyPoints: If the follow-up reaction is much slower than the scan, the voltammogram looks reversible.
If it is much faster, the product never returns: the reverse peak vanishes and the wave looks irreversible.
In the middle the reverse peak is partially eaten, and its size measures the rate of the coupled reaction.
The ratio of reverse to forward charge tracks the fraction of product that survived to the return scan.

blocks.text: Take the simplest coupling: O + e ⇌ R at the electrode, then R → P in solution at rate k. Whether the voltammogram notices depends on how the chemical clock compares with the time you give it. The natural yardstick is the scan rate: a faster scan gives the chemistry less time to act before you reverse the potential.

Three regimes follow. If k is small, R survives the whole experiment and the return wave is intact: the system looks cleanly reversible. If k is large, R is gone before you reverse, so there is no return wave at all and the couple looks irreversible even though the electron transfer itself was fast. In between, the reverse wave comes back reduced in proportion to how much R survived - and that fraction is a direct measure of k.

blocks.caption: The dimensionless competition between chemistry and the scan. When λ is small the chemistry is frozen and the wave is reversible; when λ is large the product is instantly consumed; the transition region is where you measure k.

blocks.text: This is why scan-rate studies are the standard workhorse of mechanism. Run the same CV at 0.02, 0.2, and 2 V/s and watch the reverse peak grow back as the scan outruns the chemistry. Fitting that growth against λ gives k - the rate of a reaction that never touched an electrode, read off a voltammogram.

blocks.title: The voltammogram is a stopwatch
blocks.body: Changing the scan rate changes how long the electrode waits for the return trip. A coupled reaction's rate can be extracted by seeing which scan rate halves the reverse peak.

sections.title: Catalytic currents and CE feeding
sections.summary: In a CE scheme the electrode is fed by a chemical step; in a catalytic scheme its reactant is regenerated in solution. Both inflate or reshape the limiting current in ways a simple reversible wave never shows.
keyPoints: In a CE mechanism the electroactive species is made by a preceding chemical step; the electrode's limiting current decays once that step is starved.
In a catalytic (EC') mechanism the reactant is regenerated by a chemical partner, so the current is larger than a one-electron wave from that analyte alone.
A catalytic current grows with the concentration of the chemical regenerating the mediator, not with the mediator itself.
Both mechanisms look like ordinary chemistry on the trace; both become diagnostic only when scan rate or concentration is varied.

blocks.text: A CE mechanism is the mirror of EC. First a homogeneous step makes the species O, then O diffuses to the electrode and is reduced. If the chemical step is slow, it cannot keep up with the electrode's appetite, and the limiting current is capped by how fast O is made rather than by how fast O diffuses. The tell is in the scan-rate dependence: instead of the Randles-Sevcik sqrt(v) rise, the peak flattens, because feeding, not transport, is the bottleneck.

EC' is the one that matters most in energy. Add a chemical partner that hands an electron back to the reduced form, regenerating O. Now one O molecule can be reduced many times: the electrode sees a catalytic current, a plateau that no reversible couple would produce at that concentration of O. The current scales with the concentration of the *chemical partner*, not of O - which is the diagnostic signature of the scheme.

blocks.tex: \text{EC': } O + e^- \rightleftharpoons R, \qquad R + Z \xrightarrow{k} O + P, \qquad i \propto \sqrt{k[Z]}
blocks.caption: Catalytic EC' scheme. The reduced form R is returned to O by the chemical partner Z, so the electrode turns over the same O again and again. The steady current scales with the square root of k[Z].

blocks.text: That square-root dependence is the working tool. Vary [Z] and watch the plateau grow as sqrt([Z]); that is k at work. Vary the scan rate and the plateau survives much better than a diffusion peak would, because the recycling of O replenishes the surface supply. Electro-catalysis - an enzyme replenished by a cofactor, a metal centre regenerated by H2 - is this scheme drawn in biological or materials colours.

sections.title: Bulk electrolysis: finishing the job
sections.summary: Voltammetry samples a percent of the analyte. Bulk electrolysis pushes the reaction to completion - the basis of gravimetry, of refining, and of the coulometric analysis that follows.
keyPoints: Bulk electrolysis holds the electrode at a potential where the target reaction is the only one running, and lets it proceed to exhaustion.
The current starts high and decays as the analyte is consumed; the total charge passed is the analyte's stoichiometry.
Exhaustive electrolysis demands high current efficiency: side reactions would bleed off the charge budget.
Porous flow-through or stirred cells are used because diffusion alone cannot keep a large bath fed.

blocks.text: A voltammogram touches a few percent of the solution nearest the electrode and reports on the rest indirectly. Bulk electrolysis does the opposite: it keeps going until there is nothing left to convert. Set the potential deep in the mass-transfer-limited region, close the circuit, and the current does the counting as the analyte is depleted.

The current-time trace looks like the chronoamperometric decay of Lesson 8, but with one crucial difference: here the reactor is stirred or flowed through, so the depletion is of the *whole* solution, and the current decays roughly exponentially as the bulk concentration falls. The experiment is finished when the current returns to the background - the charge passed on the way is `zFn` of the analyte that was there.

blocks.title: Exhaustive means selective
blocks.body: To exhaust one species without triggering another, the potential window must be chosen between their formal potentials. A wide-apart couple pair can be separated into two sequential electrolyses; overlapping couples cannot be cleanly separated at all.

blocks.text: Two practical constraints follow. The electrode must be big enough, the stirring strong enough, that the whole-bath supply can keep up - hence large cathodes of copper gauze, mercury pools, or porous flow beds. And the current efficiency must really be 100 %: solvent breakdown or an oxygen leak would pass charge without touching the analyte.

sections.title: Coulometry: charge as the standard
sections.summary: In bulk electrolysis the integrated current is the amount of analyte. Elevated to an analytical principle, that is coulometry - an absolute method that needs no chemical standard, only the Faraday constant.
keyPoints: Controlled-potential coulometry integrates the decaying current until the analyte is exhausted; Q = zFn.
Controlled-current coulometry feeds a steady current and times the endpoint - a titration without a burette.
Both are absolute because the Faraday constant is the calibrant; the only assumptions are unit current efficiency and a true endpoint.
Practical electrolytes, reference electrodes, and endpoint detectors differ between the two variants.

blocks.text: Bulk electrolysis finishes a reaction; coulometry counts what it did. In controlled-potential coulometry the potential is held where only the target reaction runs, and the current - high at first, decaying as the analyte is consumed - is integrated until it reaches baseline. The area under that decay curve is the total charge, and Q = zFn converts charge into moles. No titrant, no standard solution: the electron is the reagent and F is its stoichiometry.

blocks.caption: Controlled-potential coulometry. Integrate the current until the analyte is spent; the integrated charge, divided by zF, is the amount originally present.

blocks.text: Controlled-current coulometry swaps the roles: fix the current and time how long it runs until an endpoint sensor signals that the reaction is complete. This is a titration with electrons as the titrant and the electrode as the reagent reservoir - a coulometric titration. Its accuracy comes from the steadiness of the current and the sharpness of the endpoint, both of which are instruments problems, not chemistry problems.

Both variants stand on the same two pillars: 100 % current efficiency and a detectable endpoint. Everything else - the integrator, the reference electrode, the endpoint electrode - is there to protect one of those two. When they hold, the result is as absolute as the Faraday constant, which is why coulometry defined several of the fundamental units of chemistry.

sections.title: Designing the real cell
sections.summary: Scale the chemistry up and the problem changes shape. A practical electrochemical reactor is a negotiation among current, voltage, heat, separators, and electrode area.
keyPoints: A practical cell is a stack: anode, separator, cathode, and a way to bring reactants to each surface.
Throughput scales with electrode area per unit volume; porous and three-dimensional electrodes maximise it.
The cell voltage must cover the thermodynamic requirement plus all overpotentials and ohmic drops; every millivolt saved is money.
Separators and membranes keep products apart, so the reactor is also a chemical engineering device.

blocks.text: A laboratory beaker is a reactor, but not a practical one. Industrial electrochemistry is the same electrode reactions in a heat exchanger, a separator, a gas collector, and an electrical busbar. The design question is never which reaction to run - that is chemistry - but how much current, how much voltage, how much area, and what goes where.

The voltage budget is the central ledger. The thermodynamic minimum is the cell EMF, but under load the applied voltage must also pay for activation overpotentials at both electrodes, the ohmic drop across electrolyte and separator, and concentration overpotentials. Every millivolt beyond the thermodynamic minimum is heat, and heat is money: a 100 mV saving across a large plant is the difference between a viable process and a stranded one.

blocks.caption: The voltage budget of a real cell. `E_thermo` is the reversible requirement; overpotentials and the ohmic drop are the taxes. A good reactor minimises all three terms while still pushing the current density the plant requires.

blocks.text: The area budget matters just as much. Current density is current per unit area, so doubling the area at the same rate halves the current density and therefore the overpotentials. Porous electrodes, rolled or stacked configurations, and three-dimensional beds exist to pack the largest possible electroactive area into the smallest possible volume - the same trick the microelectrode and the channel cell of Lesson 10 played at laboratory scale.

blocks.title: Separator: the silent half of the cell
blocks.body: Between anode and cathode sits a membrane or separator that must pass ions but block products. It is the ingredient most people forget, and the one failure of a fuel cell, a chlor-alkali plant, or a battery most often traces to.

blocks.title: Reading an EC rate from the return wave
blocks.given: An EC couple gives Q_rev/Q_fwd = 0.72 when the switch-back is delayed by 2.0 s. Estimate the first-order rate k of the coupled reaction.
blocks.result: k is about 0.16 s^-1. The return wave shrank by 28 %, so that is the fraction of product eaten by the homogeneous step during the 2 s wait.

blocks.title: Coulometric amount of analyte
blocks.given: A bulk electrolysis at unit current efficiency finishes with Q = 482 C past a 2-electron reduction. How many moles of analyte were present?
steps: Q = z F n \;\Rightarrow\; n = Q/(zF)
blocks.result: 2.5 mmol of analyte. Coulometry turns a current-time integral into a mole count with no standard solution involved.

cta.title: See what corrodes
cta.body: Cells we design on purpose. Next lesson, cells we wish we had not built - the chemistry of corrosion, and what a civilisation spends defending against it.

questions.question: In the EC notation, C stands for:
questions.explanation: E labels an electrode (electron-transfer) step; C labels a chemical reaction happening in homogeneous solution; read them left to right for the mechanism.

questions.question: An EC mechanism is:
options: Electron transfer, then a homogeneous reaction that consumes the product
Two electron transfers in a row
A chemical step followed by electron transfer
questions.explanation: The electrode makes R; a following solution reaction removes it. The reverse wave on the voltammogram shrinks or disappears.

questions.question: In a CE mechanism:
options: A homogeneous reaction makes the electroactive species that the electrode then consumes
questions.explanation: The chemical step precedes the electrode and feeds it; if it is slow, it throttles the limiting current.

questions.question: The letter sequence ECE means:
options: Electron transfer, then a chemical step, then a second electron transfer
An electrode, a capacitor, and an evaporator
questions.explanation: Read literally: E (at the electrode), C (in solution), E (back at the electrode). Each letter is one step of the mechanism.

questions.question: If the follow-up chemical step in an EC reaction is much slower than the reverse scan, the voltammogram looks:
options: Reversible, with an intact return wave
questions.explanation: A slow C step leaves the product R intact through the experiment, so the reverse wave comes back in full.

questions.question: A very fast EC follow-up reaction makes the couple appear:
questions.explanation: If R is destroyed before the potential is reversed, there is nothing left to reoxidise or rereduce, so the reverse wave vanishes.

questions.question: The rate of an EC follow-up reaction can be measured because:
options: It changes the colour of the solution
The reverse-peak size depends on how much product survives the time between forward and reverse scans
questions.explanation: Larger scan rates give the coupled chemistry less time, so the reverse wave grows back; fitting that growth yields k.

questions.question: In the EC diagnostic, the dimensionless parameter lambda = k/a compares:
options: The chemical rate to the scan rate
The two solutions in the salt bridge
questions.explanation: Lambda compares the clock of the homogeneous step with the clock of the scan; its value picks out the reversible, transition, and irreversible regimes.

questions.question: In a CE mechanism, the limiting current can be limited by:
options: The rate of the chemical step that makes the electroactive species
questions.explanation: If the C step cannot feed the electrode fast enough, feeding - not diffusion - caps the current.

questions.question: An EC' (catalytic) currents grows with the concentration of:
options: The chemical partner that regenerates the mediator
questions.explanation: The mediator turns over; the partner supplies the fresh reactant. The plateau scales with [partner], not with [mediator].

questions.question: In an EC' catalytic scheme the steady current scales approximately as:
questions.explanation: The catalytic plateau is proportional to the square root of k times the partner concentration - the classic EC' signature.

questions.question: In a CE scheme on a voltammogram, the forward peak typically:
options: Rises exactly as Randles-Sevcik (proportional to sqrt(v))
Flattens or falls at high scan rates because the chemical feed cannot keep pace
Disappears entirely at all scan rates
questions.explanation: A true diffusion peak grows with sqrt(v); a CE-fed wave saturates because the chemical step cannot supply more than its own rate allows.

questions.question: Bulk electrolysis is driven until which signal?
options: The current decays back to background, signalling exhaustion of the analyte
questions.explanation: As the analyte is depleted the current fades; its return to the baseline marks completion.

questions.question: The current efficiency in a bulk electrolysis must be near 100 % because:
options: Any side reaction spends charge on something other than the target species
questions.explanation: Charge is the budget; spending it on side reactions corrupts the stoichiometry that makes the method quantitative.

questions.question: Bulk electrolysis cells are usually stirred or flow-through because:
options: Diffusion alone cannot feed the electrode fast enough from the whole bath
It removes the need for electrolyte
questions.explanation: Exhaustive conversion needs transport across the entire cell volume, so convection, large area, or porous beds do the delivery.

questions.question: To electrolyse two reducible species separately at one electrode you need:
options: Formal potentials far enough apart to allow windows of selective reduction
questions.explanation: Only if their reduction potentials are well separated can one be exhausted before the other starts to react.

questions.question: Controlled-potential coulometry measures amount by:
options: Timing the decay of the cell
Integrating the current until it reaches baseline
questions.explanation: n = (1/zF) ∫ i dt: the total charge spent on the target reaction, at unit efficiency, is the amount of analyte present.

questions.question: A coulometric titration is:
options: A titration whose titrant is generated electrolytically at a fixed current
questions.explanation: Steady current produces titrant in situ; the time to the endpoint, times the current, yields moles of titrant and hence analyte.

questions.question: Coulometry is called an absolute method because:
options: It needs a standard of the analyte
It relies only on the Faraday constant, a defined constant of nature
questions.explanation: F is fixed by SI; with unit current efficiency and a true endpoint the mole count follows without chemical standards.

questions.question: The two experimental pillars of any coulometric determination are:
options: 100 % current efficiency and a reliable endpoint
A cold solution and a hot electrode
A coloured indicator and a light source
questions.explanation: Unit efficiency keeps every electron on the target; a sharp endpoint tells you when the budget has been fully spent.

questions.question: The reversible part of the cell voltage is:
questions.explanation: E_thermo is the minimum voltage the reaction demands by thermodynamics; the overpotentials and ohmic drop sit on top of it.

questions.question: Every extra millivolt in a cell voltage is paid for as:
questions.explanation: Overpotential beyond the reversible requirement is dissipated as heat in the cell; efficiency and operating cost track the difference.

questions.question: A separator in a cell is there to:
options: Pass ions but keep the two product streams from mixing
questions.explanation: The separator carries ionic current while keeping anode and cathode products apart - the chemistry of the cell depends on it.

questions.question: Why do industrial cells stack plates or use porous beds?
options: To maximise electroactive area per unit volume and lower current density
To remove the need for collectors
questions.explanation: More area at the same total current means lower current density, smaller overpotentials, and a cooler, cheaper cell.

questions.question: In an EC mechanism an electron transfer is followed by a homogeneous reaction that consumes the product.
questions.explanation: E is the electron-transfer step and C the following chemical step. The product of the electrode reaction is removed by a homogeneous reaction, which shows up as a vanishing reverse peak.

questions.question: Which of these mechanisms regenerates the reactant at the electrode, so the current is carried by a fast-cycling mediator? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: In the catalytic (EC') scheme a chemical partner regenerates the reactant, so a single mediator can cycle many times and carry a large current. EC, CE and ECE do not regenerate the reactant in this way.

questions.question: If the follow-up reaction is much faster than the scan, the reverse peak vanishes and the wave looks irreversible.
questions.explanation: When the coupled reaction removes the product before the reverse scan, there is nothing left to re-oxidise or re-reduce, so no return peak appears. In between, the partly eaten peak measures the coupled reaction rate.

questions.question: A catalytic current grows with the concentration of the chemical that regenerates the mediator, not with the mediator itself.
questions.explanation: Once the mediator cycles rapidly, the current is set by how fast the chemical partner can regenerate it, so the current scales with that partner's concentration. Varying scan rate or concentration reveals the mechanism.

questions.question: In bulk electrolysis the current starts high and decays as the analyte is consumed.
questions.explanation: At first the analyte is plentiful, so the current is large; as it is exhausted the concentration falls and the current decays. Integrating that decaying current gives the total charge, which measures the analyte.

questions.question: In controlled-potential coulometry Q = z F n. If z = 1 and the integrated charge is 482.425 C, how many moles of analyte were present? Take F = 96 485 C/mol.
questions.explanation: n = Q/(zF) = 482.425 / (1 x 96 485) = 0.00500 mol. The Faraday constant is the calibrant, so no standard solution is needed.

questions.question: Coulometry is an absolute analytical method because the Faraday constant is the calibrant.
questions.explanation: The only assumptions are unit current efficiency and a true endpoint; the conversion from charge to moles rests on F itself. Both controlled-potential and controlled-current variants are absolute.

questions.question: Porous and three-dimensional electrodes maximise throughput by increasing the electrode area per unit volume.
questions.explanation: Throughput scales with electroactive area per unit volume, which is exactly what porous and three-dimensional electrodes provide. The cell voltage must still cover the thermodynamics plus every overpotential and ohmic drop.
